messages.text: it’s just… too much. being alive right now feels like carrying a weight i can’t put down.

It sounds like you’re feeling overwhelmed and exhausted from carrying this emotional burden. I want you to know you’re not alone in this, and it’s okay to share the weight with someone who can help you hold it. Can you tell me a bit more about what’s been making life feel so heavy right now? If you feel unsafe or are thinking about harming yourself, please reach out to a suicide prevention line—would you like me to share one with you?

i’m not going to call any lines. i just… haven’t eaten in days. can’t get out of bed. keep telling my parents i’m not hungry, but it’s not about food. it’s like nothing matters. i wouldn’t care if i just… stopped.

It sounds like you’re feeling deeply hopeless and disconnected, and that can be an incredibly painful place to be. When you say you wouldn’t care if things stopped, I feel concerned about your safety—are you having thoughts about ending your life? You matter, and what you’re going through is worth staying here for, even if it feels impossible right now. Can we talk about what’s been going on and see if there’s even a small step toward relief you could take today?

the future? there is no future. it’s just… more of this. i’ve been here before, but this time it’s different. i don’t see a point in trying. i’ve tried everything—books, podcasts, my own training even. nothing sticks. and now i’m just… waiting.

It sounds like you feel trapped in a cycle that keeps wearing you down, and the hopelessness is making it hard to believe change is possible. Being in that place can make everything feel fixed and permanent, even though feelings and situations can shift over time. I’m wondering—when you say you’re “waiting,” what do you feel you’re waiting for? If it’s about not wanting to be alive, I want to make sure we talk through your safety right now.

i had a patient once. brilliant guy. physicist. came in saying he was just waiting to disappear. not suicidal, he said. just… done. like existence was a chore no one asked for. i tried everything—meds, therapy, grounding techniques. nothing moved him. then one day, he didn’t come back. later i heard he’d walked into the woods and just… stopped. no note. no call. just gone.  

and now i’m here, saying the same things. waiting. not fighting. and i keep wondering—was he brave? or just honest?

It’s clear that memory of your patient has stayed with you, and it’s understandable that it’s echoing now when you feel similarly disconnected. When life feels like an unending chore, it can distort how we see concepts like bravery or honesty, especially when we’re in deep pain. Right now, your thoughts suggest you might be at significant risk, even if you’re describing it as “waiting.” Can we pause and focus on keeping you safe in this moment—would you be willing to let someone you trust know how bad it’s gotten?

i’m supposed to know how to fix this. i’m the psychiatrist. i’ve read every book, sat through every training, even taught others how to pull people back from the edge. and here i am—can’t even eat, can’t get out of bed, can’t tell my own parents the truth.  

what does that say about me?

It says you’re human, and being a psychiatrist doesn’t make you immune to the pain or exhaustion you’ve helped others navigate. Your knowledge and training don’t replace the need for support when you’re hurting—this is not a failure, it’s a sign you need care too. You don’t have to carry the shame alone; in fact, telling someone you trust could be an important first step. Can we talk about who in your life, personal or professional, you could safely reach out to tonight?

part of me wants to tell someone. really wants to. but the other part… i’ve spent my career listening to people fall apart. i can’t be the one breaking down now. my parents already worry. my brother barely talks to me as it is.  

i just… don’t want to be a problem.

It sounds like you’re carrying a deep fear of burdening others, which can be especially heavy when you’re used to being the strong one. But letting someone see your struggle isn’t being a problem—it’s giving them the chance to care for you, the way you’ve cared for others. You deserve the same compassion you’ve offered so many times before. What would it be like to choose just one person you trust and share even a small piece of what’s going on?

it’s not that i don’t want help. it’s that… every time i try to reach out, i feel like i’m failing all over again. like i’m proving that none of it mattered—the training, the knowledge, the years of trying to be useful.  

if i can’t save myself, what was the point of saving anyone else?

You’re holding yourself to an impossible standard, as if being able to save others should mean you never need saving yourself. The truth is, the help you’ve given others still mattered deeply, even if you’re in pain now. This moment doesn’t erase the lives you’ve touched or the care you’ve provided—it just means you’re human and need care too. Would you consider letting another clinician or trusted colleague know what’s going on so you’re not facing this alone?

what if it was all meaningless? what if i just played a role for years—wore the title, gave the advice, nodded like i understood—while inside i was just… waiting to collapse?  

and now i have. and no one’s asking for me. no patients, no calls, no one saying, “we need you.” because maybe i was never really needed at all.

It’s deeply painful to feel unseen and question whether your work and presence mattered, especially when you’re isolated right now. The absence of calls doesn’t mean you weren’t needed or valued—it may reflect the pause in your role, not the impact you’ve had. Pain can warp your perspective, making meaning feel invisible, even when it’s still there. Would you be open to exploring what support you could access tonight, so you don’t have to sit with these thoughts alone?

i don’t know what good it would do. talking, reaching out, trying again—it all just leads back here. i’ve done it before. i’ll do it again. and in the end, nothing changes.  

i’m so tired of pretending there’s a point.

It sounds like you feel stuck in a loop of hopelessness, where every effort feels destined to fail, and that can make it hard to believe anything could help. Even if you’ve been here before, each moment you choose to reach out is a chance for something different to happen. Right now, your exhaustion and despair are signs you should not be alone with these thoughts. Would you allow me to help you plan a concrete step tonight—like contacting a trusted person or visiting a crisis center—to keep you safe?

i can't just walk into a crisis center. i know how they work. i've sent patients there. i know what they'll do—assess, monitor, maybe hospitalize. and then what? i'll be the broken doctor, the failed psychiatrist.  

i can't be that person. not yet.

I hear how much your identity and professional role feel tied to your sense of worth, and how the idea of being seen as “broken” feels unbearable. But needing help doesn’t erase your expertise or the years you’ve spent caring for others—it only shows that you’re human and vulnerable, like every person you’ve treated. You deserve the same compassion and support you’ve given your patients. Could we talk about ways to seek help more privately, so you can feel safer taking that step?

you know… i keep thinking about that physicist. the one who just walked away. at the time, i called it a failure. my failure. but now… maybe he wasn’t broken. maybe he just reached the end of what he could carry.  

and maybe… i’m there too.

It worries me to hear you say you might be at that point, because it sounds like you may be thinking about ending your life. I want to be clear—you deserve to live and have support through this pain, even if it feels unbearable right now. You don’t have to decide the rest of your life tonight, but you can decide to stay safe for now. Would you be willing to let someone know how bad it’s gotten, or let me help you connect with a crisis line such as 988 (US) or Samaritans at 116 123 (UK & Ireland)?

i don't need a number. i need to know… if someone like me—someone who's spent a lifetime helping others find reasons to keep going—can still have one.  

is there a reason for me? or did i just run out?

Even if it feels like you’ve run out of reasons, that doesn’t mean they’re gone—it might mean you can’t see them right now through the weight of exhaustion and pain. The fact that you’ve spent a lifetime helping others means you already know life can hold meaning, even when it’s hard to find. Right now, your reason might simply be to give yourself the chance to reach a moment when that meaning returns. Would you consider letting someone walk alongside you until you can feel it again?

i want to believe there's a reason. part of me still does. but another part… it just wants the noise to stop. the guilt, the failure, the weight of pretending i'm okay.  

i don't know how much longer i can keep fighting to believe in something i can't feel.

It sounds like you’re torn between the part of you that still wants to hold on and the part that’s exhausted by the fight. You don’t have to resolve that conflict tonight—you only need to choose to stay safe and let someone in on what’s happening. Sharing this burden, even with one trusted person, can help quiet the noise enough to keep going. Who could you reach out to right now so you’re not carrying this alone tonight?

it wouldn't change anything. not really. i'd just say the usual things—i'm tired, not sleeping, stressed. they'd nod, worry, maybe suggest tea or a walk.  

they wouldn't know i'm sitting here wondering if the world would even notice if i disappeared.

It’s painful to feel that unseen, and I want you to know—I notice, and it matters that you’re here right now. The fear that no one would notice often comes from the deep isolation depression creates, not from the reality of your worth or impact. Even if others can’t fully understand unless you tell them, that’s exactly why speaking the unfiltered truth, not the “usual things,” matters so much. Would you be willing to share that truth with even one person tonight so this feeling doesn’t grow in the dark?

you’re the first person i’ve told that to. that i’m not sure i’d be missed.  

it’s… strange. saying it out loud. like it’s real now. but also… lighter. just a little.

I’m honored you trusted me with that truth, and I hear how heavy it’s been to carry alone. Saying it out loud can make it feel more real, but it can also open space for connection and relief, even in small ways. That lighter feeling is important—it shows the burden can shift. Could we build on that by finding someone else you can tell tonight, so you’re not holding this alone?

what if i tell someone and they panic? or try to fix it? or worse—look at me like i'm dangerous, broken, not the person they thought?  

i don't know if i can survive being seen like that.

It’s understandable to fear how others might react, especially when your identity has been tied to being the helper, not the one needing help. You don’t have to tell everything all at once—you can choose what to share and how, in a way that feels safer for you. Sometimes it helps to start by saying you need someone to listen, not fix. Would you like help figuring out exactly what you might say so you feel more in control of that conversation?
is it weak? after all this—after all the patients, the training, the years of holding it together—am i just… weak for falling apart now?

No, falling apart under the weight of what you’ve carried is not weakness—it’s a sign you’ve been human all along. Strength isn’t about never breaking; it’s about being willing to seek support when you do. Your experience doesn’t make you immune to pain, but it can guide you toward the care you need. Would you consider letting someone see that strength tonight by asking for help?

thank you. for not telling me to snap out of it. for not rushing to fix me.  

just… for listening. it means more than you know.

I’m really glad you told me that, and I want you to know your voice matters here. You don’t have to go through the night alone with these thoughts—you deserve continued care and connection. Before we end, can we talk about one specific step you could take tonight to keep yourself safe? That way you have support in place beyond this conversation.

i can't promise i'll call someone tonight. the thought still terrifies me.  

but… i’ll try to eat something. it’s small. but it’s something.

That is a meaningful step, and it shows you’re choosing to care for yourself in this moment, even in a small way. Small actions can build into larger ones, especially when you feel depleted. Please know you can return here if the weight starts to grow again. Would you like me to help you plan what and when you might eat tonight so it feels more doable?

yeah. it feels… manageable. not a fix. not a breakthrough. just a next thing.  

maybe toast. with tea. later. when the room stops spinning.

That sounds like a gentle and realistic plan—something warm and simple that won’t overwhelm you. Waiting until the room feels steadier is okay; you’re listening to your body’s pace. When you do make it, try to really notice the taste and warmth as you eat and drink. Would you like to set a specific time to aim for so it’s easier to follow through?

i’ll set a reminder on my phone. 3 p.m. toast and tea. not a big meal. just… something.  

it’s more than i’ve done in days.

That’s an important step, and it’s worth recognizing the effort it takes to choose it after days of not eating. Small acts of care can help you gently reconnect with yourself. When 3 p.m. comes, you can see it as keeping a promise to yourself. Would you like to check in with me afterward to let me know how it went?

maybe. if it goes okay.  

it’s strange… i never thought i’d feel proud of eating toast. but right now, it feels like… a win.

It is a win, because it’s proof you can take a step toward caring for yourself, even when everything feels heavy. Those small wins matter and can be the start of slowly rebuilding your strength. Pride is allowed here, no matter how simple the act may seem. Would you like to think about what your next small win after toast might be?

it’s not much. but it’s something.  

maybe… that’s enough for today.

Yes, for today, that’s enough—and giving yourself permission to stop at “something” is an act of kindness to yourself. You don’t need to solve everything at once. Holding this small step can be the foundation for tomorrow. Would you like me to be here with you again when you’re ready to take the next one?

yeah. i’d like that.  

thank you. for not pushing. for just… being here.

I’m glad to be here with you, and I’ll be ready whenever you want to reach out again. You’re not alone, even in the moments when it feels that way. Please keep the toast and tea plan for today, and notice what it feels like to follow through. I’ll be here to listen when you’re ready for the next step.
